The hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{prop:fourier} are now met with $k=d$, $\eta=1/2(\log N)^{1/100}$, and $K=MN^{-2/\log \log N}$. This yields some $S\subset A'\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1/d_j$ as required. Otherwise, Proposition~\ref{prop:tech_iterative} yields some $B\subset A'$ such that \[R(B)\geq 2/3d_j-1/M\geq 1/2d_j+(\log N)^{-1/200}\] and where $\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_B}\frac{1}{q}\leq \frac{2}{3}\log\log N$. We apply Lemma~\ref{lem:techmainprec} again, with $y=4d$ and $w=z$, to produce some corresponding $B'\subset B$ and $d'\in [4d,z]$. Since $\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_{B'}}\frac{1}{q}\leq \sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_B}\frac{1}{q}\leq \frac{2}{3}\log\log N$ we can apply Proposition~\ref{prop:tech_iterative2}. The hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{prop:fourier} are now met with $k=d'$ and $\eta,K$ as above, and thus there is some $S\subset B'\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1/d'$ as required.
nodes.name: Proof of Main Technical Proposition
nodes.statement_short: Apply the precursor lemma, then either the Fourier proposition directly or after one iteration via the iterative propositions.

nodes.name: Expand omega squared
nodes.statement: Since $\omega(n) = \sum_{p\leq n}1_{p\mid n}$, the left-hand side is equal to, after expanding the sum and rearranging, \[\sum_{p,q\leq X}\sum_{n\leq X}1_{p\mid n}1_{q\mid n}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Expand $\omega(n)^2$ as a double sum over primes

nodes.name: Diagonal terms
nodes.statement: The part of the sum where $p=q$ is \[\sum_{p\leq X}\sum_{n\leq X}\lfloor X/p\rfloor = X\log\log X+O(X),\] as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:omegasum}.

nodes.name: Off-diagonal terms
nodes.statement:
If $p
eq q$, then $p\mid n$ and $q\mid n$ if and only if $pq\mid n$, and so the sum over $n$ is bounded above by \[\sum_{n\leq X}1_{pq\mid n}= \lfloor X/pqfloor \leq X/pq.\] Therefore \[\sum_{\substack{p,q\leq X\ p
eq q}}\sum_{n\leq X}1_{p\mid n}1_{q\mid n}\leq X\sum_{\substack{p,q\leq X\ p
eq q}} rac{1}{pq}\leq X\sum_{p,q\leq X} rac{1}{pq}\leq X rac{\sum_{p\leq X} rac{1}{p}}^2.\]

nodes.name: Apply Mertens
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:mertensprimes} this is $X(\log\log X+O(1))^2 = X(\log\log X)^2+O(X\log\log X)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Mertens for primes to the off-diagonal bound

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement: The lemma follows by combining the estimates on the two parts of the sum.

nodes.name: Expand square
nodes.statement: The left-hand side equals \[\sum_{n\leq X}\omega(n)^2 - 2\log\log X\sum_{n\leq X}\omega(n)+\lfloor X\rfloor (\log\log X)^2.\]
nodes.statement_short: Expand the square into three summands

nodes.name: First summand
nodes.statement: The first summand is at most, by Lemma~\ref{lem:omegasquaredsum}, \[X(\log\log X)^2 +O(X\log\log X).\]
nodes.statement_short: Bound first summand by the omega-squared lemma

nodes.name: Second summand
nodes.statement: The second summand is equal to, by Lemma~\ref{lem:omegasum}, \[-2\log\log X(X\log\log X+O(X)) = -2X(\log\log X)^2 +O(X\log\log X).\]
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate second summand by the omega-sum lemma

nodes.name: Third summand
nodes.statement: The third summand is equal to \[(X+O(1))(\log\log X)^2 = X(\log\log X)^2 + O(X\log\log X).\]

nodes.name: Main terms cancel
nodes.statement: Therefore the main terms cancel, and \[\sum_{n\leq X}(\omega(n) - \log\log X)^2\leq O(X\log\log X)\] as required.

nodes.name: Auxiliary bound tau(n) <= n^{1/K} K^{2^K}
nodes.statement: We first show that, for any real $K\geq 2$, \[\tau(n) \leq n^{1/K}K^{2^K}.\] Write $n$ as the product of unique prime powers $n=p_1^{k_1}\cdots p_r^{k_r}$, so that \[\frac{\tau(n)}{n^{1/K}} = \frac{\prod_{i=1}^r (k_i+1)}{\prod_{i=1}^r p_i^{k_i/K}} = \prod_{i=1}^r \frac{k_i+1}{p_i^{k_i/K}}.\] If $p_i>2^K$ then \[\frac{k_i+1}{p_i^{k_i/K}}\leq \frac{k_i+1}{2^{k_i}}\leq 1,\] since $1+k \leq 2^k$ for all integer $k\geq 0$ by Bernoulli's inequality. Therefore \[ \prod_{i=1}^r \frac{k_i+1}{p_i^{k_i/K}} \leq \prod_{\substack{1\leq i\leq r\\ p_i<2^K}}\frac{k_i+1}{p_i^{k_i/K}}.\] If $p_i<2^K$ then, since $p_i\geq 2$, \[\frac{k_i+1}{p^{k_i/K}}\leq \frac{k_i+1}{2^{k_i/K}}\leq \frac{k_i+1}{k_i/K+1/2},\] using the fact that $x+1/2\leq 2^x$ for all $x\geq 0$. Since $K\geq 2$ the denominator here is $\geq (1+k_i)/K$, and so $\frac{k_i+1}{p^{k_i/K}}\leq K$. Therefore \[\frac{\tau(n)}{n^{1/K}}\leq \prod_{\substack{1\leq i\leq r\\ p_i<2^K}} K\leq K^{\pi(2^K)}\leq K^{2^K},\] as required.

nodes.name: Factorise n
nodes.statement: Write $n$ as the product of unique prime powers $n=p_1^{k_1}\cdots p_r^{k_r}$, so that \[\frac{\tau(n)}{n^{1/K}} = \frac{\prod_{i=1}^r (k_i+1)}{\prod_{i=1}^r p_i^{k_i/K}} = \prod_{i=1}^r \frac{k_i+1}{p_i^{k_i/K}}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Factorise $n$ and write $\tau(n)/n^{1/K}$ as a product

nodes.name: Large primes
nodes.statement: If $p_i>2^K$ then \[\frac{k_i+1}{p_i^{k_i/K}}\leq \frac{k_i+1}{2^{k_i}}\leq 1,\] since $1+k \leq 2^k$ for all integer $k\geq 0$ by Bernoulli's inequality. Therefore \[ \prod_{i=1}^r \frac{k_i+1}{p_i^{k_i/K}} \leq \prod_{\substack{1\leq i\leq r\\ p_i<2^K}}\frac{k_i+1}{p_i^{k_i/K}}.\]

nodes.name: Small primes
nodes.statement: If $p_i<2^K$ then, since $p_i\geq 2$, \[\frac{k_i+1}{p^{k_i/K}}\leq \frac{k_i+1}{2^{k_i/K}}\leq \frac{k_i+1}{k_i/K+1/2},\] using the fact that $x+1/2\leq 2^x$ for all $x\geq 0$. Since $K\geq 2$ the denominator here is $\geq (1+k_i)/K$, and so $\frac{k_i+1}{p^{k_i/K}}\leq K$.

nodes.name: Combine factors
nodes.statement: Therefore \[\frac{\tau(n)}{n^{1/K}}\leq \prod_{\substack{1\leq i\leq r\\ p_i<2^K}} K\leq K^{\pi(2^K)}\leq K^{2^K},\] as required.
nodes.statement_short: At most $\pi(2^K)\le 2^K$ factors of size $\le K$

nodes.name: Choose K
nodes.statement: The second part of the proof is to apply the first part with \[K=\brac{1+\epsilon/2}^{-1}\frac{\log\log n}{\log 2}.\] (The right-hand side tends to $\infty$ as $n\to\infty$, so for sufficiently large $n$ we have $K\geq 2$ as required.)

nodes.name: Estimate 2^K and log K
nodes.statement: Note that $2^K= (\log n)^{\frac{2}{2+\epsilon}}\leq (\log n)^{1-\epsilon}$ (since $1-\epsilon>\frac{2}{2+\epsilon}$, since $\epsilon\leq 1$) and \[\log K \leq \log\log\log n.\]

nodes.name: Take logarithms
nodes.statement: Taking logarithms of the inequality in the first part, \[\log \tau(n) \leq \frac{\log n}{K}+2^K\log K\leq \log n\brac{\frac{1}{K}+\frac{\log\log\log n}{(\log n)^\epsilon}}\] \[= \log n\frac{\log 2}{\log\log n}\brac{1+\epsilon/2+\frac{(\log\log\log n)(\log\log n)}{(\log 2)(\log n)^{\epsilon}}}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Take logs of the auxiliary bound

nodes.name: Absorb error
nodes.statement: For any fixed $\epsilon>0$, the function $\frac{(\log\log\log n)(\log\log n)}{(\log 2)(\log n)^{\epsilon}}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty$, so for sufficiently large $n$ it is $\leq \epsilon/2$, and hence \[\log \tau(n) \leq \log n\frac{\log 2}{\log\log n}(1+\epsilon)\] as required.

nodes.name: Introduce P
nodes.statement: Let $P = \prod_{u\leq p\leq v}p$. The left-hand side of the estimate in the lemma can be written as \[\sum_{x\leq n<x+y}1_{(n,P)=1}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the count as coprimality to $P$

nodes.name: Möbius inversion
nodes.statement: Using the identity $\sum_{d\mid m}\mu(d) = 1$ if $m=1$ and $0$ otherwise, the fact that $d\mid (n,P)$ if and only if $d\mid n$ and $d\mid P$, and that $\sum_{n\leq z}1_{d\mid n}=\left\lfloor\frac{z}{d}\right\rfloor$ for any $z\geq 0$, \[ \sum_{x< n\leq x+y}1_{(n,P)=1}= \sum_{x< n\leq x+y}\sum_{d\mid (n,P)}\mu(d)\] \[= \sum_{x< n\leq x+y}\sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\ d\mid P}}\mu(d)\] \[=\sum_{d\mid P}\mu(d)\sum_{x< n\leq x+y}1_{d\mid n}\] \[=\sum_{d\mid P}\mu(d)\left(\left\lfloor \frac{x+y}{d}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{x}{d}\right\rfloor\right).\]
nodes.statement_short: Expand via Möbius inversion and swap sums

nodes.name: Floor approximation
nodes.statement: Since $\lfloor X\rfloor = X+O(1)$ for any $X$, we have \[\left\lfloor \frac{x+y}{d}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{x}{d}\right\rfloor=\frac{y}{d}+O(1)\] for any $x,y,d$, and hence \[\sum_{x< n\leq x+y}1_{(n,P)=1}=y\sum_{d\mid P}\frac{\mu(d)}{d}+O(\sum_{d\mid P}1).\]

nodes.name: Error term
nodes.statement: We have $\sum_{d\mid P}1=\tau(P)=2^k$ where $k$ is the number of primes in $[u,v]$, which is at most $v$, so the error term here is $O(2^v)$.

nodes.name: Euler product
nodes.statement: Finally, expanding out the product shows that \[\sum_{d\mid P}\frac{\mu(d)}{d} = \prod_{p\in[u,v]}\brac{1-\frac{1}{p}}.\] Inserting this into the above finishes the proof.

nodes.name: Set parameters
nodes.statement: Suppose $A\subset \bbn$ has upper density $\delta>0$. Let $y=C_1/\delta$ and $z=\delta^{-C_2\delta^{-2}}$, where $C_1,C_2$ are two absolute constants to be determined later.

nodes.name: Reduce to R(S)=1/d
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that there is some $d\in [y,z]$ and finite $S\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1/d$.

nodes.name: Iterate removal
nodes.statement: Indeed, given such an $S$ we can remove it from $A$ and still have an infinite set of upper density $\delta$, so we can find another $S'\subset A\backslash S$ with $R(S')=1/d'$ for some $d'\in [y,z]$, and so on.
nodes.statement_short: Repeatedly remove such sets keeping upper density

nodes.name: Pigeonhole on d
nodes.statement: After repeating this process at least $\lceil z-y\rceil^2$ times there must be some $d\in [y,z]$ with at least $d$ disjoint $S_1,\ldots,S_d\subset A$ with $R(S_i)=1/d$. Taking $S=S_1\cup\cdots \cup S_d$ yields $R(S)=1$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Pigeonhole gives $d$ disjoint sets with sum $1/d$, union sums to 1

nodes.name: Choose N
nodes.statement: By definition of the upper density, there exist arbitrarily large $N$ such that $\abs{A\cap [1,N]}\geq \frac{\delta}{2}N$.

nodes.name: Discard large prime powers
nodes.statement: The number of $n\in [1,N]$ divisible by some prime power $q\geq N^{1-6/\log\log N}$ is \[\ll N \sum_{N^{1-6/\log\log N}<q\leq N}\frac{1}{q}\ll \frac{N}{\log\log N}\] by Mertens' estimate Lemma~\ref{lem:mertens1}.
nodes.statement_short: Mertens: few $n$ have a large prime-power divisor

nodes.name: Discard atypical omega
nodes.statement: Further, by Tur\'{a}n's estimate Lemma~\ref{lem:turan} \[\sum_{n\leq N}(\omega(n)-\log\log N)^2 \ll N \log\log N,\] the number of $n\in [1,N]$ that do not satisfy \begin{equation} \tfrac{99}{100}\log\log N\leq \omega(n) \leq 2\log\log N \end{equation} is $\ll N/\log\log N$.

nodes.name: Sieve condition
nodes.statement: Finally, provided we choose $C_2$ sufficiently large in the definition of $z$, Lemma~\ref{lem:sieve2} ensures that the proportion of all $n\in \{1,\ldots,N\}$ not divisible by at least two distinct primes $p_1,p_2\in [y,z]$ with $4p_1<p_2$ is at most $\frac{\delta}{8}N$, say.
nodes.statement_short: Sieve Estimate 2: few $n$ lack two spaced primes in $[y,z]$

nodes.name: Define A_N
nodes.statement: In particular, provided $N$ is chosen sufficiently large (depending only on $\delta$), we may assume that $\abs{A_N}\geq \frac{\delta}{4}N$, where $A_N\subset A$ is the set of those $n\in A\cap [N^{1-1/\log\log N},N]$ which satisfy conditions (2)-(4) of Proposition~\ref{prop:techmain}.

nodes.name: Lower bound R(A_N)
nodes.statement: Since $\abs{A_N}\geq \frac{\delta}{4}N$, \[R(A_N) \gg -\log(1-\delta/4)\gg \delta.\] In particular, since $y=C_1/\delta$ for some suitably large constant $C_1>0$, we have that $R(A_N)\geq 4/y$, say.

nodes.name: Apply main technical proposition
nodes.statement: All of the conditions of Proposition~\ref{prop:techmain} are now satisfied (provided $N$ is chosen sufficiently large in terms of $\delta$), and hence there is some $S\subset A_N\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1/d$ for some $d\in [y,z]$, which suffices as discussed above.

nodes.name: Set epsilon
nodes.statement: Let $C\geq 2$ be an absolute constant to be chosen shortly, and for brevity let $\epsilon = \log\log\log N/\log\log N$, so that we may assume that $R(A)\geq C\epsilon \log N$.

nodes.name: Restrict to large n
nodes.statement: Since $\sum_{n\leq X}\frac{1}{n}\ll \log X$, if $A'=A\cap [N^\epsilon,N]$ we have (assuming $C$ is sufficiently large) $R(A')\geq \frac{C}{2}\epsilon\log N$.

nodes.name: Remove sieved integers
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be those integers $n\in [1,N]$ not divisible by any prime $p\in [5,(\log N)^{1/1200}]$. Lemma~\ref{lem:sieve1} implies that, for any $x\geq \exp(\sqrt{\log N})$, \[\abs{X\cap[x,2x)}\ll \frac{x}{\log\log N}\] and hence, by partial summation, \[\sum_{\substack{n\in X\\ n\in [\exp(\sqrt{\log N}),N]}}\frac{1}{n}\ll \frac{\log N}{\log\log N}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Sieve Estimate 1: integers without small primes contribute little

nodes.name: Remove atypical omega
nodes.statement: Similarly, if $Y$ is the set of those $N\in [1,N]$ such that $\omega(n) <\frac{99}{100}\log\log N$ or $\omega(n)\geq \frac{101}{100}\log\log N$ then Tur\'{a}n's estimate Lemma~\ref{lem:turan} \[\sum_{n\leq x}(\omega(n)-\log\log n)^2\ll x\log\log x\] implies that $\abs{Y\cap [x,2x)}\ll x/\log\log N$ for any $N\geq x\geq \exp(\sqrt{\log N})$, and so \[\sum_{\substack{n\in Y\\ n\in [\exp(\sqrt{\log N}),N]}}\frac{1}{n}\ll \frac{\log N}{\log\log N}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Turán: integers with atypical $\omega$ contribute little

nodes.name: Remaining mass
nodes.statement: In particular, provided we take $C$ sufficiently large, we can assume that $R(A'\backslash (X\cup Y))\geq \frac{C}{4}\epsilon \log N$, say.
nodes.statement_short: Remaining set keeps reciprocal sum $\ge C\epsilon\log N/4$

nodes.name: Dyadic-type decomposition
nodes.statement: Let $\delta=1-1/\log\log N$, and let $N_i=N^{\delta^i}$, and $A_i=(A'\backslash (X\cup Y))\cap [N_{i+1},N_i]$. Since $N_i\leq N^{e^{-i/\log\log N}}$ and $A'$ is supported on $n\geq N^\epsilon$, the set $A_i$ is empty for $i> \log(1/\epsilon)\log\log N$, and hence by the pigeonhole principle there is some $i$ such that \[R(A_i)\geq \frac{C}{8}\frac{\epsilon\log N}{(\log\log N)\log(1/\epsilon)}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Split into ranges $[N_{i+1},N_i]$ and pigeonhole one

nodes.name: Check conditions
nodes.statement: By construction, $A_i\subset [N_{i+1},N_i]\subset [N_i^{1-1/\log\log N_i},N_i]$, and every $n\in A_i$ is divisible by some prime $p$ with $5\leq p\leq (\log N)^{1/1200}\leq (\log N_i)^{1/500}$. Furthermore, every $n\in A_i$ satisfies $\omega(n)\geq \frac{99}{100}\log\log N\geq \frac{99}{100}\log\log N_i$ and $\omega(n)\leq \frac{101}{99}\log\log N\leq 2\log\log N_i$.
nodes.statement_short: $A_i$ satisfies the range, small-prime and $\omega$ conditions

nodes.name: Remaining task
nodes.statement: Finally, it remains to discard the contribution of those $n\in A_i$ divisible by some large prime power $q> N_i^{1-6/\log\log N_i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Remains to discard large prime powers

nodes.name: Large prime power contribution
nodes.statement: The contribution to $R(A_i)$ of all such $n$ is at most \[ \sum_{N_i^{1-6/\log\log N_i}< q\leq N_i}\sum_{\substack{n\leq N_i\\ q\mid n}}\frac{1}{n} \ll \sum_{N_i^{1-6/\log\log N_i}< q\leq N_i}\frac{\log(N_i/q)}{q}\] \[\ll \frac{\log N_i}{\log\log N_i}\sum_{N_i^{1-6/\log\log N_i}<q\leq N_i}\frac{1}{q}\ll \frac{\log N}{(\log\log N)^2},\] using Lemma~\ref{lem:mertens1}.
nodes.statement_short: Contribution of large prime powers via Mertens

nodes.name: Define A_i'
nodes.statement: Provided we choose $C$ sufficiently large, this is $\leq R(A_i)/2$, and hence, if $A_i'\subset A_i$ is the set of those $n$ divisible only by prime powers $q\leq N_i^{1-6/\log\log N_i}$, then $R(A_i')\geq (\log N)^{1/200}$, say.

nodes.name: Apply corollary
nodes.statement: All of the conditions of Corollary~\ref{cor:tech_cor} are now met, and hence there is some $S\subset A_i'\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1$, as required.

nodes.name: Maximal disjoint family
nodes.statement: Let $k$ be maximal such that there are disjoint $S_1,\ldots,S_k\subset A$ where, for each $1\leq i\leq k$, there exists some $d_i\in [1,(\log N)^{1/500}]$ such that $R(S_i)=1/d_i$. Let $t(d)$ be the number of $S_i$ such that $d_i=d$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a maximal family of disjoint $S_i$ with $R(S_i)=1/d_i$

nodes.name: Enough sets with same d
nodes.statement: If there is any $d$ with $t(d)\geq d$ then we are done, taking $S$ to be the union of any $d$ disjoint $S_j$ with $R(S_j)=1/d$.
nodes.statement_short: If $t(d)\ge d$, union of $d$ of them works

nodes.name: Few sets
nodes.statement: Otherwise, \[\sum_i R(S_i)= \sum_{1\leq d\leq (\log N)^{1/500}} \frac{t(d)}{d}\leq (\log N)^{1/500},\] and hence if $A'=A\backslash (S_1\cup\cdots \cup S_k)$ then $R(A')\geq (\log N)^{1/500}$.

nodes.name: Apply main proposition
nodes.statement: We may now apply Proposition~\ref{prop:techmain} with $y=1$ and $z=(\log N)^{1/500}$ -- note that condition (2) of Proposition~\ref{prop:techmain} follows from condition (2) of the hypotheses with $d_1=1$ and $d_2=p\in [5,(\log N)^{1/500}]$ some suitable prime divisor.

nodes.name: Contradiction with maximality
nodes.statement: Thus there exists some $S'\subset A'$ such that $R(S')=1/d$ for some $d\in [1,(\log N)^{1/500}]$, contradicting the maximality of $k$.

nodes.name: Apply Eratosthenes-Legendre
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:sieve_eratosthenes} yields \[\abs{X\cap [N,2N)} = \prod_{y\leq p\leq z}\brac{1-\frac{1}{p}}N+ O(2^z).\]

nodes.name: Apply Mertens product
nodes.statement: Mertens' estimate \ref{lem:mertens2} yields \[\prod_{p\leq z}\brac{1-\frac{1}{p}}^{-1} \gg \log z\] and \[\prod_{p\leq y}\brac{1-\frac{1}{p}}^{-1} \ll \log y,\] whence \[\prod_{y\leq p\leq z}\brac{1-\frac{1}{p}}^{-1}\gg \frac{\log z}{\log y},\] and hence \[ \prod_{y\leq p\leq z}\brac{1-\frac{1}{p}}\ll \frac{\log y}{\log z}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Mertens bounds the product by $\log y/\log z$

nodes.name: Main term
nodes.statement: Therefore the first term above is $\ll \frac{\log y}{\log z}N$.

nodes.name: Error term
nodes.statement: The second term is \[\ll 2^z \leq 2^{\log N}=N^{\log 2}\ll \frac{N}{\log N}\ll \frac{\log y}{\log z}N,\] and the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Error term is negligible since $z\le\log N$

nodes.name: No prime in [w,z]
nodes.statement: Let $w\in (4y,z)$ be some parameter to be chosen later. Lemma~\ref{lem:sieve1} implies that the number of $n\in \{1,\ldots,N\}$ not divisible by any prime $p\in [w,z]$ is $\ll \frac{\log w}{\log z}N$.
nodes.statement_short: Sieve Estimate 1 bounds integers with no prime in $[w,z]$

nodes.name: No close smaller prime
nodes.statement: Similarly, for any $p\in [w,z]$, the number of those $n\in [1,N]$ divisible by $p$ and no prime $q\in [y,p/4)$ is \[\ll \frac{\log y}{\log p}\frac{N}{p}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Count $n$ divisible by $p$ but no prime in $[y,p/4)$

nodes.name: Combine counts
nodes.statement: It follows that the number of $n\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\backslash Y$ is \[\ll \brac{\frac{\log w}{\log z}+ \log y\sum_{p\geq w}\frac{1}{p\log p}}N.\]

nodes.name: Partial summation
nodes.statement: By partial summation, $\sum_{p\geq w}\frac{1}{p\log p}\ll 1/\log w$, and hence \[\abs{ \{1,\ldots,N\}\backslash Y}\ll \brac{\frac{\log w}{\log z}+\frac{ \log y}{\log w}}N.\]

nodes.name: Optimise w
nodes.statement: Choosing $w=\exp\brac{\sqrt{(\log y)(\log z)}}$ completes the proof.

nodes.name: Case m divides n
nodes.statement: If $m\mid n$ then $n/m$ is an integer, so $e(hn/m)=1$ for all $h\in \mathbb{Z}$, so the right-hand side is $1$.

nodes.name: Case m does not divide n
nodes.statement:
If $m
mid n$ then $e(n/m)
eq 1$. Let $S=\sum_{h\in I}e(hn/m)$, so it suffices to show that $S=0$. Using $e(x+y)=e(x)e(y)$ we have \[e(n/m)S = \sum_{h\in I}e((h+1)n/m).\] If $r=\min(I)$ and $s=\max(I)$ then the right-hand side is $S + e((s+1)n/m)-e(rn/m)$. But since $I$ is a set of $m$ consecutive integers we know that $s=r+m-1$, and so \[e((s+1)n/m)-e(rn/m) = e(rn/m+n)-e(rn/m)=e(rn/m)e(n)-e(rn/m)=0,\] since $e(n)=1$. Therefore $e(n/m)S=S$, and hence since $e(n/m)
eq 1$, this forces $S=0$ as required.

nodes.name: Introduce S
nodes.statement: Let $S=\sum_{h\in I}e(hn/m)$, so it suffices to show that $S=0$.

nodes.name: Shift sum
nodes.statement: Using $e(x+y)=e(x)e(y)$ we have \[e(n/m)S = \sum_{h\in I}e((h+1)n/m).\]
nodes.statement_short: Multiply by $e(n/m)$ to shift the sum

nodes.name: Telescoping
nodes.statement: If $r=\min(I)$ and $s=\max(I)$ then the right-hand side is $S + e((s+1)n/m)-e(rn/m)$.
nodes.statement_short: Shifted sum differs by boundary terms

nodes.name: Boundary terms cancel
nodes.statement: But since $I$ is a set of $m$ consecutive integers we know that $s=r+m-1$, and so \[e((s+1)n/m)-e(rn/m) = e(rn/m+n)-e(rn/m)=e(rn/m)e(n)-e(rn/m)=0,\] since $e(n)=1$.

nodes.name: S vanishes
nodes.statement: Therefore $e(n/m)S=S$, and hence since $e(n/m)\neq 1$, this forces $S=0$ as required.

nodes.name: Primes of lcm lie in P_A
nodes.statement: We first note that if $p\mid [A]$ then $p\in \mathcal{P}_A$. If not, suppose $p\not\in\mathcal{P}_A$ and $p\mid [A]$. Let $M=[A]/p$. We claim every $n\in A$ divides $M$, contradicting the definition of lowest common multiple. It suffices to show that if a prime power $q^r\mid n$ then $q\mid M$. But we know $q^r\mid [A]=Mp$, and $(q^r,p)=1$, so $q\mid M$ as required.

nodes.name: Assume otherwise
nodes.statement: If not, suppose $p\not\in\mathcal{P}_A$ and $p\mid [A]$. Let $M=[A]/p$.

nodes.name: Every n divides M
nodes.statement: We claim every $n\in A$ divides $M$, contradicting the definition of lowest common multiple. It suffices to show that if a prime power $q^r\mid n$ then $q\mid M$. But we know $q^r\mid [A]=Mp$, and $(q^r,p)=1$, so $q\mid M$ as required.

nodes.name: Reduce to prime powers
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that if a prime power $q^r\mid n$ then $q\mid M$.

nodes.name: Coprimality
nodes.statement: But we know $q^r\mid [A]=Mp$, and $(q^r,p)=1$, so $q\mid M$ as required.

nodes.name: Factorise lcm
nodes.statement: By the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, we can write $[A] = \prod_{p\in \mathcal{P}_A}p^{s_p}$ for some integers $s_p\geq 0$.

nodes.name: Remaining
nodes.statement: It remains to show that $s_p=r_p$.

nodes.name: Lower bound s_p
nodes.statement: That $s_p\geq r_p$ follows from the fact that $p^{r_p}\mid n$ for some $n\in A$ by definition, hence $p^{r_p}\mid [A]$, hence $r_p\leq s_p$.

nodes.name: Upper bound s_p
nodes.statement: Suppose that $s_p>r_p$, and as above consider $M=[A]/p$. We claim every $n\in A$ divides $M$, the required contradiction. If a prime power $q^r\mid n$ with $q\neq p$ then $q\mid Mp$ hence $q\mid M$. If $p^r\mid n$ then $r\leq r_p$, so $p^r\mid p^{r_p}\mid p^{s_p-1}\mid M$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: If $s_p>r_p$ then $[A]/p$ is a smaller common multiple

nodes.name: Other primes
nodes.statement: If a prime power $q^r\mid n$ with $q\neq p$ then $q\mid Mp$ hence $q\mid M$.

nodes.name: The prime p
nodes.statement: If $p^r\mid n$ then $r\leq r_p$, so $p^r\mid p^{r_p}\mid p^{s_p-1}\mid M$, as required.

nodes.name: lcm factorisation
nodes.statement: We have $[A]=\prod_{p\in\mathcal{P}_A}p^{r_p}$, where $p^{r_p}\in \mathcal{Q}_A$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:lcm_desc}.

nodes.name: Bound by X^{|P_A|}
nodes.statement: By hypothesis $p^{r_p}\leq X$ and so $[A]\leq X^{\abs{\mathcal{P}_A}}$.

nodes.name: Chebyshev
nodes.statement: The set $\mathcal{P}_A$ is a subset of all primes $\leq X$, and so $\abs{\mathcal{P}_A}\leq \pi(X)\ll X/\log X$ by Chebyshev's estimate Lemma~\ref{lem:chebyshev}.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore \[[A]\leq X^{O(X/\log X)}=e^{O(X)}.\]

nodes.name: Jordan's inequality
nodes.statement: We have Jordan's inequality, which says $\sin(\pi x)\geq 2x$ for all $x\in[0,1/2]$. Therefore \[\cos(\pi x)^2 = 1-\sin(\pi x)^2\leq 1-4x^2.\]

nodes.name: Exponential bound
nodes.statement: Since $1-y\leq e^{-y}$ for all $y\geq 0$, the right-hand side is $\leq e^{-4x^2}$.

nodes.name: Square roots
nodes.statement: Taking square roots, and using $\cos(\pi x)\geq 0$ for all $x\in[0,1/2]$, yields \[\cos(\pi x) \leq e^{-2x^2}.\]

nodes.name: Product divides n
nodes.statement: The first step is to show that $\prod_{q\in\mathcal{Q}(n)}q\mid n$ (in fact they're equal, but all we need is the one direction). This can be shown by showing that every $q\in\mathcal{Q}(n)$ divides $n$, since $n\in A_q$ implies $q\mid n$, and then noting that any two distinct $q_1,q_2\in \mathcal{Q}(n)$ are coprime. If not, then since they are prime powers, they must both be powers of the same prime, say $q_1=p^{r_1}< q_2=p^{r_2}$. Since $n\in A_{q_2}$ we have $p^{r_2}\mid n$, but then $p\mid n/q_1$, so $p\mid (q_1,n/q_1)$, and so $n\not\in A_{q_1}$.

nodes.name: Divisibility and coprimality
nodes.statement: This can be shown by showing that every $q\in\mathcal{Q}(n)$ divides $n$, since $n\in A_q$ implies $q\mid n$, and then noting that any two distinct $q_1,q_2\in \mathcal{Q}(n)$ are coprime.
nodes.statement_short: Each $q$ divides $n$ and distinct $q$ are coprime

nodes.name: Coprimality
nodes.statement: If not, then since they are prime powers, they must both be powers of the same prime, say $q_1=p^{r_1}< q_2=p^{r_2}$. Since $n\in A_{q_2}$ we have $p^{r_2}\mid n$, but then $p\mid n/q_1$, so $p\mid (q_1,n/q_1)$, and so $n\not\in A_{q_1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Two powers of the same prime contradict the definition of $A_q$

nodes.name: Product bound
nodes.statement: Therefore $\prod_{q\in\mathcal{Q}(n)}q\leq n$.
nodes.statement_short: Product of the $q$ is at most $n$

nodes.name: Take logs
nodes.statement: Since all prime powers are $\geq 2$ it follows that $2^{\abs{\mathcal{Q}(n)}}\leq n$, and the result follows taking logarithms.

nodes.name: Clear denominators
nodes.statement: For any $S\subset A$, $k\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}\in \bbz$ if and only if $k\sum_{n\in S}\frac{[A]}{n}\in [A]\cdot \bbz$.

nodes.name: Integrality
nodes.statement: By definition $n\mid [A]$ for all $n\in A$, and so $k\sum_{n\in S}\frac{[A]}{n}$ is an integer. It is $\geq 0$ since each summand is.
nodes.statement_short: The scaled sum is a non-negative integer

nodes.name: Orthogonality
nodes.statement: Therefore by Lemma~\ref{lem:orthogonality}, if $I$ is any set of $[A]$ consecutive integers \[1_{k\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}\in \bbz}=1_{[A]\mid k\sum_{n\in S}\frac{[A]}{n}} = \frac{1}{[A]}\sum_{h\in I}e(kh\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}).\]

nodes.name: Swap sums
nodes.statement: Therefore, changing summation, \[F(A;k) = \sum_{S\subset A}1_{k\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}\in \bbz} = \frac{1}{[A]} \sum_{h\in I}\sum_{S\subset A}\prod_{n\in S}e(kh/n).\]

nodes.name: Product expansion
nodes.statement: The lemma now follows choosing $I=(-[A]/2,[A]/2]\cap\bbz$, and using the general fact that for any indexed set of complex numbers $(x_i)_{i\in I}$ \[\sum_{J\subset I}\prod_{j\in J}x_j = \prod_{i\in I}(1+x_i).\]
nodes.statement_short: Expand subset sums as a product

nodes.name: Range of kR(S)
nodes.statement: For any $S\subset A$ we have $k\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}\leq kR(A)<2$, and therefore if $k\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n} \in \bbn$ then $k\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n} =0$ or $=1$.

nodes.name: Exclude 1
nodes.statement: The latter can't happen by assumption, so $k\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n} =0$.

nodes.name: Only empty set
nodes.statement: A non-empty sum of $>0$ summands is $>0$, so if $k\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}\in \bbz$ then $S=\emptyset$. Therefore $F(A;k)=1$.

nodes.name: Apply orthogonality formula
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:orthog_rat} therefore \[1=\frac{1}{[A]}\sum_{-[A]/2< h\leq [A]/2}\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(kh/n)).\]

nodes.name: Take real parts
nodes.statement: The conclusion follows multiplying both sides by $[A]$ and taking real parts of both sides.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply by $[A]$ and take real parts

nodes.name: Apply identity
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:orthog_simp} \[\sum_{-[A]/2< h\leq [A]/2}\Re\brac{\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(kh/n))}= [A].\]

nodes.name: Use lcm bound
nodes.statement: By assumption the right-hand side is $\leq 2^{\abs{A}-1}$.

nodes.name: h=0 term
nodes.statement: When $h=0$ \[\Re\brac{\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(kh/n))}= \Re\brac{\prod_{n\in A}2}=2^{\abs{A}}.\]

nodes.name: Rearrange
nodes.statement: Therefore \[\sum_{h\in J(A)}\Re\brac{\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(kh/n))}+2^{\abs{A}}\leq 2^{\abs{A}-1},\] and the result follows after rearranging.

nodes.name: Assume overlap
nodes.statement: Suppose not and $h\in \mathfrak{M}(t_1)\cap \mathfrak{M}(t_2)$.

nodes.name: Triangle inequality
nodes.statement: By definition, \[\abs{hk-t_1[A]}\leq K/2\] and \[\abs{hk-t_2[A]}\leq K/2,\] and so by the triangle inequality $[A]\abs{t_1-t_2}\leq K$.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: Since $t_1\neq t_2$, we know $\abs{t_1-t_2}\geq 1$, and so $[A]\leq K$, contradicting the assumption.

nodes.name: Parametrise arc
nodes.statement: Since $k$ divides $[A]$, we know that $t[A]/k$ is an integer for any $t\in \bbz$, and hence by definition of $\mathfrak{M}(t)$ we can write $h=t[A]/k+r$, where $r$ is an integer satisfying $\abs{r}\leq K/2k$.

nodes.name: Shift to r
nodes.statement: Therefore, letting \[J_t =[-K/2k,K/2k]\cap (J(A)-t[A]/k),\] then \[\sum_{h\in \mathfrak{M}(t)}\Re\brac{\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(kh/n))}=\sum_{r\in J_t}\Re\brac{\prod_{n\in A}(1+e((t[A]+rk)/n))}=\sum_{r\in J_t}\Re\brac{\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(rk/n))},\] since $t[A]/n$ is always an integer, by definition of $[A]$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite each arc sum over $r\in J_t$

nodes.name: Cosine rewrite
nodes.statement: Using Lemma~\ref{lem:useful_rewrite}, this is \[2^{[A]}\sum_{h\in \mathfrak{M}(t)}\cos(\pi krR(A))\prod_{n\in A}\cos(\pi kr/n).\]
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite as a product of cosines

nodes.name: Arcs disjoint
nodes.statement: Since $[A]\geq \min(A)\geq M>K$, the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:majorarcs_disjoint} are all met, and so $\mathfrak{M}$ is the disjoint union of $\mathfrak{M}(t)$ as $t$ ranges over $t\in \bbz$.

nodes.name: Rearrange sum
nodes.statement: Therefore $1_{h\in\mathfrak{M}}=\sum_t 1_{h\in \mathfrak{M}(t)}$, and therefore using the above and rearranging the sum, \[\sum_{h\in \mathfrak{M}(A,k,K)}\Re\brac{\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(kh/n))} =\sum_{r\in [-K/2k,K/2k]\cap\bbz}\brac{\sum_{t\in \bbz}1_{r\in J_t}}\cos(\pi krR(A))\prod_{n\in A}\cos(\pi kr/n).\]

nodes.name: Cosines nonnegative
nodes.statement: Since for all $n\in A$ we have $n\geq M>K$ we have $\abs{kr/n}< 1/2$ for all $r$ with $\abs{r}\leq K/2k$, and hence $\cos(\pi kr/n)\geq 0$ for all such $n$ and $r$.

nodes.name: Phase cosine nonnegative
nodes.statement: Furthermore, writing $kR(A)=2-\epsilon$ for some $0<\epsilon\leq k/M$, we have (since $r$ is an integer) \[\cos(\pi kr R(A)) = \cos(-\pi r\epsilon)\geq 0,\] since $\abs{r\epsilon}\leq K/2M<1/2$ for all $\abs{r}\leq K/2k$.

nodes.name: Sum nonnegative
nodes.statement: It follows that \[\brac{\sum_{t\in \bbz}1_{r\in J_t}}\cos(\pi krR(A))\prod_{n\in A}\cos(\pi kr/n)\geq 0\] for all $r\in [-K/2k,K/2k]\cap \bbz$, and hence as the sum of non-negative summands the original sum is non-negative as required.

nodes.name: Full sum negative
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:orthog_simp2} \[\sum_{h\in J(A)}\Re\brac{\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(kh/n))}\leq -2^{\abs{A}-1}.\]

nodes.name: Major arcs nonnegative
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:majorarcs} \[\sum_{h\in \mathfrak{M}(A,k,K)}\Re\brac{\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(kh/n))} \geq 0.\]

nodes.name: Minor arcs negative
nodes.statement: Therefore \[\sum_{h\in J(A)\backslash \mathfrak{M}(A,k,K)}\Re\brac{\prod_{n\in A}(1+e(kh/n))}\leq -2^{\abs{A}-1}.\]

nodes.name: Triangle inequality
nodes.statement: By the triangle inequality, using $\abs{\Re z}\leq \abs{z}$ and $\abs{1+e(\theta)}=2\cos(\pi \theta)$, \[\sum_{h\in J(A)\backslash \mathfrak{M}(A,k,K)}\abs{\cos(\pi kh/n)} \geq 1/2\] as required.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to absolute values of cosines

nodes.name: Pointwise bound suffices
nodes.statement: We show in fact that for any $h\in \mathfrak{m}_1(A,k,K,T)$ we have \[C(A;hk)\leq 1/[A]^2.\] The result then immediately follows since $\abs{\mathfrak{m}_1(A,k,K,T)}\leq \abs{J(A)}\leq [A]$, assuming $[A]\geq 8$, which is true since $[A]\geq \min(A)\geq M\geq 8$.

nodes.name: Cosine product bound
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:cos_prod_bound}, \[C(A;hk)\leq \exp\brac{-\frac{2}{N^2}\sum_{n\in A}h_n^2},\] where $kh\equiv h_n\pmod{n}$ and $\abs{h_n}\leq n/2$.

nodes.name: Interval I_h
nodes.statement: Let $I_h$ be the interval of length $K$ centred around $kh$. If no element of $I_h$ is divisible by $n$ then $\abs{h_n}>K/2$.

nodes.name: Many large residues
nodes.statement: Therefore, by definition of $\mathfrak{m}_1$, $\abs{h_n}>K/2$ for at least $T$ many $n\in A$, and hence $\sum_{n\in A}h_n^2\geq K^2T/4$, and so \[C(A;h)\leq \exp\brac{-\frac{K^2T}{2N^2}}.\]

nodes.name: Compare with lcm
nodes.statement: It remains to note that by Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth_lcm} \[[A]\leq \exp\brac{O\brac{\frac{K^2T}{N^2\log N}}}\leq \exp\brac{\frac{K^2T}{4N^2}}\] assuming $N$ is sufficiently large.

nodes.name: Redistribute product
nodes.statement: For any $n\in A$, let $\mathcal{Q}(n)$ denote all those $q\in \mathcal{Q}$ such that $n\in A_q$. Therefore, for any real $x_n\geq 0$, \[\prod_{n\in A}x_n=\prod_{n\in A}\prod_{q\in \mathcal{Q}(n)}x_n^{1/\abs{\mathcal{Q}(n)}} =\prod_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}\prod_{n\in A_q}x_n^{1/\abs{\mathcal{Q}(n)}}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite product over $n$ as product over $q$

nodes.name: Bound |Q(n)|
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:triv_q_bound} for any $n\in A$ we have $\abs{\mathcal{Q}(n)}\leq \tfrac{1}{\log 2}\log n\leq 2\log N$, and so if $0\leq x_n\leq 1$, \[\prod_{n\in A}x_n\leq \prod_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}\prod_{n\in A_q}x_n^{1/2\log N}=\prod_{q\in \mathcal{Q}}\brac{\prod_{n\in A_q}x_n}^{1/2\log N}.\] In particular, \[C(A;t)\leq \prod_{q\in \mathcal{Q}}C(A_q;t)^{/2\log N}.\] Using the trivial bound $C(A_q;t)\leq 1$, to prove the lemma it therefore suffices to show that for every $q\in\mathcal{Q}\backslash\mathcal{D}_h$ we have $C(A_q;t)\leq N^{-8\log N}$.

nodes.name: Residues t_n
nodes.statement: For any $n\in A$ let $t\equiv t_n\pmod{n}$, where $\abs{t_n}\leq n/2$. For any $q\in\mathcal{Q}\backslash \mathcal{D}$ there are, by definition of $\mathcal{D}$, at least $L/q$ many $n\in A_q$ such that $n$ divides no element of the interval of length $K$ centred at $t$.
nodes.statement_short: Many $n\in A_q$ divide nothing in the interval

nodes.name: Recall t_n
nodes.statement: Recall that $t_n$ is the integer in $(-n/2,n/2]$ such that $t\equiv t_n\pmod{n}$, so that $n$ divides $t-t_n$.

nodes.name: Large residues
nodes.statement: If $\abs{t_n}\leq K/2$ then $t-t_n$ is in the interval of length $K$ centred at $t$, which contradicts the previous paragraph. Therefore $\abs{t_n}>K/2$.

nodes.name: Cosine product bound
nodes.statement: Hence by Lemma~\ref{lem:cos_prod_bound} \[C(A_q;t)\leq\exp\brac{-\frac{2}{N^2}\cdot \frac{L}{q}\cdot \frac{K^2}{4}}.\]

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: By assumption, $q\leq LK^2/16N^2(\log N)^2$, and the proof is complete.

nodes.name: Interval I_h
nodes.statement: For any $h\in\mathfrak{m}_2$, let $I_h$ be the interval of length $K$ centred at $kh$.

nodes.name: Use dichotomy
nodes.statement: Since $h\not\in\mathfrak{m}_1$, condition 2(a) cannot hold, and therefore there is some $x\in I_h$ divisible by all $q\in\mathcal{D}_{I_h}(A;L)$. In particular, $kh$ is distance at most $K/2$ from some multiple of $[\mathcal{D}_{I_h}(A;L)]$.
nodes.statement_short: Hypothesis 2(b) holds: $kh$ near a multiple of $[\mathcal{D}_{I_h}]$

nodes.name: Not major arc
nodes.statement: Since $h\in \mathfrak{m}(A,k,K,T)$, we know $h\not\in \mathfrak{M}(A,k,K)$, and hence $kh$ is distance greater than $K/2$ from any multiple of $[A]$.

nodes.name: D is proper
nodes.statement: Since $[\mathcal{Q}]=[A]$, it follows that $\mathcal{D}_{I_h}(A;L)\neq \mathcal{Q}$.

nodes.name: Count h per D
nodes.statement: Furthermore, for any $\mathcal{D}\subset \mathcal{Q}$, the number of $h\in\mathfrak{m}_2$ with $\mathcal{D}_{I_h}(A;L)=\mathcal{D}$ is at most $K$ times the number of multiples of $[\mathcal{D}]$ in $[1,k[A]+K]$. The number of multiples of $[\mathcal{D}]$ in $[1,k[A]+K]$ is at most $(k[A]/[\mathcal{D}])+K$, and hence the number of $h\in\mathfrak{m}_2$ with $\mathcal{D}_{I_h}(A;L)=\mathcal{D}$ is at most \[Kk\frac{[A]}{[\mathcal{D}]} +K^2\leq Kk\prod_{q\in\mathcal{Q}\backslash\mathcal{D}}q+K^2\leq kN^{\abs{\mathcal{Q}\backslash \mathcal{D}}+1}+K^2.\]

nodes.name: Count bound
nodes.statement: In particular, when $\mathcal{D}\neq \mathcal{Q}$, the right-hand side is at most $2kN^{\abs{\mathcal{Q}\backslash \mathcal{D}}+1}$, that is, \[\sum_{h\in \mathfrak{m}_2}1_{\mathcal{D}_{I_h}(A;L)=\mathcal{D}}\leq 2kN^{\abs{\mathcal{Q}\backslash \mathcal{D}}+1}.\] (Here we have used the fact that $[A]\leq [D]\prod_{q\in \mathcal{Q}\backslash \mathcal{D}}q$, which is true because every prime power dividing $[A]$ is in $\mathcal{Q}$, and hence either divides $[D]$ or divides $\prod_{q\in \mathcal{Q}\backslash \mathcal{D}}q$.)

nodes.name: Individual bound
nodes.statement: Therefore, for any $\mathcal{D}\subset\mathcal{Q}$, using Lemma~\ref{lem:minor2_ind_bound}, \[\sum_{h\in \mathfrak{m}_2}1_{\mathcal{D}_{I_h}(A;L)=\mathcal{D}}C(A;hk)\leq 2kN^{1-3\abs{\mathcal{Q}_A\backslash\mathcal{D}}}.\] Since $\mathcal{D}\neq \mathcal{Q}$, this is at most $2kN^{-1-\abs{\mathcal{Q}\backslash \mathcal{D}}}$.

nodes.name: Sum over D
nodes.statement: Therefore (using the trivial estimate $\abs{\mathcal{Q}}\leq N$) \begin{align*} \sum_{h\in\mathfrak{m}_2}C(A;h,k) &\leq \frac{2k}{N}\sum_{\mathcal{D}\subseteq\mathcal{Q}}N^{-\abs{\mathcal{Q}\backslash \mathcal{D}}}\\ &= \frac{2k}{N}(1+1/N)^{\abs{\mathcal{Q}}}\\ &\leq 8k/N \leq 1/8. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Combine arc bounds
nodes.statement: If the conclusion fails, there is an immediate contradiction by combining Lemmas~\ref{lem:minor_lbound}, \ref{lem:minor1_bound} and \ref{lem:minor2_bound}. The only hypothesis that is not immediate to check is the upper bound $[A]<2^{\abs{A}-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Minor arc lower bound contradicts the two minor arc upper bounds

nodes.name: Check lcm bound
nodes.statement: This follows since $\lvert A\rvert \geq MR(A)\geq \frac{2}{k}M-1\geq M/k$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth_lcm} we have $[A]\leq e^{O(cM/k)}$, which is at most $2^{\abs{A}/2}$ assuming $c$ is sufficiently small.
nodes.statement_short: Smooth lcm bound gives it for small $c$

nodes.name: q at most N
nodes.statement: If $q\mid (n_1,n_2)$ then $q$ divides $\abs{n_1-n_2}$, and hence in particular $q\leq N$.

nodes.name: Reduce to primes
nodes.statement: The contribution of all prime powers $p^r$ with $r\geq 2$ is $O(1)$, and hence it suffices to show that $\sum_{p\mid \abs{n_1-n_2}}\frac{1}{p}\ll \log\log\log N$. Any integer $\leq N$ is trivially divisible by $O(\log N)$ many primes. Clearly summing $1/p$ over $O(\log N)$ many primes is maximised summing over the smallest $O(\log N)$ primes.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to primes; few primes divide $|n_1-n_2|$

nodes.name: Mertens
nodes.statement: Since there are $\gg (\log N)^{3/2}$ many primes $\leq (\log N)^2$, we have \[\sum_{p\mid \abs{n_1-n_2}}\frac{1}{p}\ll \sum_{p\leq (\log N)^2}\frac{1}{p}\ll \log\log\log N\] by Mertens' estimate \ref{lem:mertens1}.
nodes.statement_short: Worst case is the smallest primes; apply Mertens

nodes.name: Multinomial bound
nodes.statement: Since, by definition, every integer $n\in A$ can be written uniquely as $q_1\cdots q_t$ for $q_i\in \mathcal{Q}_A$ for some $t\in I = [(1-\epsilon)\log\log N, 2\log\log N]$, we have that, since $t!\geq (t/e)^t$, \[R(A)\leq \sum_{t\in I}\frac{\brac{\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_A}\frac{1}{q}}^t}{t!}\leq \sum_{t\in I}\brac{\frac{e}{t}\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_A}\frac{1}{q}}^t.\]
nodes.statement_short: Bound $R(A)$ by sums of powers of $\sum 1/q$

nodes.name: Monotonicity
nodes.statement: Since $(ex/t)^t$ is decreasing in $t$ for $x<t$, either $\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_A}\frac{1}{q}\geq (1-\epsilon)\log\log N$ (and we are done), or the summand is decreasing in $t$, and hence we have \[(\log N)^{-\epsilon/2}\leq R(A)\leq 2\log\log N\brac{\frac{\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_A}\frac{1}{q}}{(1-\epsilon)e^{-1}\log\log N}}^{(1-\epsilon)\log\log N}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Either done or bound by the smallest $t$

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: The claimed bound follows, using the fact that $e^{-\frac{\epsilon}{2(1-\epsilon)}}\geq 1-\epsilon$ for $\epsilon\in (0,1/2)$, choosing $N$ large enough such that $(2\log\log N)^{2/\log\log N}\leq 1+\epsilon^2$, say.

nodes.name: Verify inequality
nodes.statement: To verify the inequality $e^{-\frac{\epsilon}{2(1-\epsilon)}}\geq 1-\epsilon$ for $\epsilon\in (0,1/2)$, note that $\frac{\epsilon}{2(1-\epsilon)}\leq \epsilon$ for all $\epsilon\in (0,1/2)$, and hence using $1+x\leq e^{x}$ for all $x\geq -1$, we have \[e^{-\frac{\epsilon}{2(1-\epsilon)}}\geq e^{-\epsilon}\geq 1-\epsilon\] as required.

nodes.name: Factorise d
nodes.statement: We can write every $d\in D$ uniquely as a product of prime powers $d=p_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}$, where for each $i$ either $r_i=1$ and $y<p_i\leq N$, or $r_i\geq 2$ and $p_i\leq N$.

nodes.name: Euler product
nodes.statement: Therefore the left-hand side is at most \[\prod_{y<p\leq N}\left(1+\frac{k}{p}\right)\prod_{p\leq N}\left(1+\frac{k}{p^2}+\cdots\right).\]

nodes.name: Square-full part
nodes.statement: The second product is, using $1+kx\leq (1+x)^k$, \[=\prod_{p\leq N}\left(1+\frac{k}{p(p-1)}\right)\leq \left(\prod_{p\leq N}\left(1+\frac{1}{p(p-1)}\right)\right)^k\leq C_1^k\] for some constant $C_1>0$, since the product converges.

nodes.name: Prime part
nodes.statement: Similarly, \[\prod_{y<p\leq N}\left(1+\frac{k}{p}\right)\leq \left(\prod_{y<p\leq N}\left(1+\frac{1}{p}\right)\right)^k,\] and the product here is $\ll (\log N/\log y)$ by Mertens' bound \ref{lem:mertens1}.

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement: Combining these yields the required estimate.

nodes.name: Fix q, y, D
nodes.statement: Fix some $q$ with $R(A;q)\geq (\log N)^{-1/2}$. Let $y=\exp((\log N)^{1-2/k})$. Let $D$ be the set of all $d$ such that if $r$ is a prime power such that $r\mid d$ and $(r,d/r)=1$ then $y<r\leq N$, and furthermore \[qd\in (M\exp(-(\log N)^{1-1/k}),N].\]

nodes.name: Covering claim
nodes.statement: We first claim that every $n\in A_q$ is divisible by some $qd$ with $d\in D$, such that $(qd,n/qd)=1$. Let $Q_n$ be the set of prime powers $r$ dividing $n$ such that $(r,n/r)=1$, so that $n=\prod_{r\in Q_n}r$. Let \[Q_n'=\{ r\in Q_n: r\neq q\textrm{ and }r>y\}.\] We let $d=\prod_{r\in Q_n'}r$. We need to check that $d\in D$ and $qd\mid n$. It is immediate from the definitions that if a prime power $r$ divides $d$ with $(r,d/r)=1$ then $r\in Q_n'$, whence $r>y$. It is also straightforward to check, by comparing prime powers, that $qd\mid n$, and hence $qd\leq n\leq N$. Furthermore, \[\frac{n}{qd}=\prod_{r\in Q_n\backslash Q_n'\cup\{q\}}r\leq y^{\abs{Q_n}}=y^{\omega(n)}\leq \exp((\log N)^{1-1/k}),\] by definition of $y$ and the hypothesis that $\omega(n)\leq (\log N)^{1/k}$. It follows that $d\in D$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Every $n\in A_q$ is divisible by some $qd$, $d\in D$

nodes.name: Construct d
nodes.statement: Let $Q_n$ be the set of prime powers $r$ dividing $n$ such that $(r,n/r)=1$, so that $n=\prod_{r\in Q_n}r$. Let \[Q_n'=\{ r\in Q_n: r\neq q\textrm{ and }r>y\}.\] We let $d=\prod_{r\in Q_n'}r$.
nodes.statement_short: Let $d$ be the product of the large prime powers of $n$ other than $q$

nodes.name: Check divisibility
nodes.statement: We need to check that $d\in D$ and $qd\mid n$. It is immediate from the definitions that if a prime power $r$ divides $d$ with $(r,d/r)=1$ then $r\in Q_n'$, whence $r>y$. It is also straightforward to check, by comparing prime powers, that $qd\mid n$, and hence $qd\leq n\leq N$.

nodes.name: Bound n/qd
nodes.statement: Furthermore, \[\frac{n}{qd}=\prod_{r\in Q_n\backslash Q_n'\cup\{q\}}r\leq y^{\abs{Q_n}}=y^{\omega(n)}\leq \exp((\log N)^{1-1/k}),\] by definition of $y$ and the hypothesis that $\omega(n)\leq (\log N)^{1/k}$.

nodes.name: d in D
nodes.statement: It follows that $d\in D$ as required.

nodes.name: Cover A_q
nodes.statement: If we let $A_q(d)=\{ n \in A_q : qd\mid n\textrm{ and }(qd,n/qd)=1\}$ then we have shown that $A_q\subseteq \bigcup_{d\in D}A_q(d)$. Therefore \[R(A;q) = \sum_{n\in A_q}\frac{q}{n}\leq \sum_{d\in D}\sum_{n\in A_q(d)}\frac{q}{n}.\]

nodes.name: Many prime factors
nodes.statement: We will control the contribution from those $d$ with $\omega(d)>\omega_0= \frac{5}{\log k}\log\log N$ with the trivial bound \[\sum_{A_q(d)}\frac{q}{n} \leq \sum_{\substack{n\leq N\\ qd\mid n}}\frac{q}{n}\leq \sum_{m\leq N}\frac{q}{dqm}\leq 2\frac{\log N}{d},\] using the harmonic sum bound $\sum_{m\leq N}\frac{1}{m}\leq \log N+1\leq 2\log N$. Therefore \[ \sum_{\substack{d\in D\\ \omega(d)>\omega_0}}\sum_{n\in A_q(d)}\frac{q}{n} \leq 2\log N\sum_{\substack{d\in D\\ \omega(d)> \omega_0}} \frac{1}{d}\] \[\leq 2k^{-\omega_0}\log N\sum_{d\in D} \frac{k^{\omega(d)}}{d}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Trivially bound $d$ with many prime factors

nodes.name: Smooth sum
nodes.statement: By \ref{lem:smoothsum} we have \[\sum_{d\in D}\frac{k^{\omega(d)}}{d}\leq \left(C\frac{\log N}{\log y}\right)^k.\] and therefore \[\sum_{\substack{d\in D\\ \omega(d)>\omega_0}}\sum_{n\in A_q(d)}\frac{q}{n}\leq 2k^{-\omega_0}\log N \left(C\frac{\log N}{\log y}\right)^k.\]
nodes.statement_short: Apply the smooth reciprocal sum bound

nodes.name: Small contribution
nodes.statement: Recalling $\omega_0=\frac{5}{\log k}\log\log N$ and $y=\exp((\log N)^{1-2/k})$ the right-hand side here is at most \[2(\log N)^{-5}C^k\leq 1/2\log N\leq \tfrac{1}{2}R(A;q),\] for sufficiently large $N$, assuming $k\leq c\log\log N$ for sufficiently small $c$.

nodes.name: Main contribution
nodes.statement: It follows that \[\tfrac{1}{2}R(A;q)\leq \sum_{\substack{d\in D\\ \omega(d)\leq \omega_0}}\sum_{d\in D}\frac{q}{n} .\]
nodes.statement_short: Half of $R(A;q)$ comes from $d$ with few factors

nodes.name: Average
nodes.statement: The result follows by averaging, since by \ref{lem:smoothsum} \[\sum_{d\in D}\frac{1}{d} \ll \frac{\log N}{\log y}\ll (\log N)^{2/k}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Average over $d$ using the smooth sum bound

nodes.name: Inductive claim
nodes.statement: We will prove the following claim, valid for any finite set $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ with $0\not\in A$ and $\epsilon>0$, via induction: for all $i\geq 0$ there exists $A_i\subseteq A$ and $Q_i\subseteq \mathcal{Q}_A$ such that \begin{enumerate} \item the sets $\mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$ and $Q_i$ are disjoint, \item $R(A_i)\geq R(A)- \epsilon\sum_{q\in Q_i}\frac{1}{q}$, \item either $i\leq \abs{A\backslash A_i}$ or, for all $q'\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$, $\epsilon < R(A_i;q')$.

nodes.name: Claim statement
nodes.statement: We will prove the following claim, valid for any finite set $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ with $0\not\in A$ and $\epsilon>0$, via induction: for all $i\geq 0$ there exists $A_i\subseteq A$ and $Q_i\subseteq \mathcal{Q}_A$ such that

nodes.name: Points (1)-(2)
nodes.statement: the sets $\mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$ and $Q_i$ are disjoint, \item $R(A_i)\geq R(A)- \epsilon\sum_{q\in Q_i}\frac{1}{q}$,
nodes.statement_short: Disjointness and reciprocal sum lower bound

nodes.name: Point (3)
nodes.statement: either $i\leq \abs{A\backslash A_i}$ or, for all $q'\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$, $\epsilon < R(A_i;q')$.
nodes.statement_short: Either progress or all local sums exceed $\epsilon$

nodes.name: Deduce lemma
nodes.statement: Given this claim, the stated lemma follows by choosing $B=A_{\abs{A}+1}$, noting that in the 5th point above the first alternative cannot hold, and furthermore \[\epsilon \sum_{q\in Q_{\abs{A}+1}}\frac{1}{q}\leq \epsilon \sum_{q\leq N}\frac{1}{q}\leq 2\epsilon \log\log N,\] by Lemma~\ref{lem:mertens1}, assuming $N$ is sufficiently large.
nodes.statement_short: Take $B=A_{|A|+1}$ and bound loss by Mertens

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: To prove the inductive claim, we begin by choosing $Q_0=\emptyset$, and $A_0=A$. All of the properties are trivial to verify.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Suppose the proposition is true for $i\geq 0$, with associated $A_i,Q_i$. We will now prove it for $i+1$. If it is true that, for all $q'\in\mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$, we have $\epsilon <R(A_i;q')$, then we let $A_{i+1}=A_i$ and $Q_{i+1}=Q_i$. Otherwise, let $q'\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$ be such that $R(A_i;q')\leq \epsilon$, set $A_{i+1} = A_i\backslash \{ n\in A_i : q'\mid n \textrm{ and }(q',n/q')=1\}$, and $Q_{i+1}=Q_i\cup \{q'\}$. It remains to verify the required properties. That $Q_{i+1}\subseteq \mathcal{Q}_A$ follows from $Q_i\subseteq \mathcal{Q}_A$ and $q'\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_i}\subseteq \mathcal{Q}_A$ (using the general fact that if $B\subseteq A$ then $\mathcal{Q}_B\subseteq \mathcal{Q}_A$). For point (1), since $A_{i+1}\subseteq A_i$, and hence $\mathcal{Q}_{A_{i+1}}\subseteq \mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$, it suffices to show that $q'\not\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_{i+1}}$. If this were not true, there would be some $n\in A_{i+1}$ such that $q'\mid n$ and $(q',n/q')=1$, contradiction to the definition of $A_{i+1}$. For point (2), we note that \[R(A_{i+1})= R(A_i)-\sum_{\substack{n\in A_i\\ q'\mid n\\ (q',n/q')=1}}\frac{1}{n} = R(A_i)-\frac{1}{q'}R(A_i;q')\geq R(A_i)-\epsilon \frac{1}{q'},\] and point (2) follows from induction and the observation that \[\frac{1}{q'}+\sum_{q\in Q_i}\frac{1}{q}=\sum_{q\in Q_{i+1}}\frac{1}{q},\] since $q'\in\mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$ and hence $q'\not\in Q_{i}$. Finally, for point (3), we note that since we assume that it is not true that for all $q'\in\mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$, we have $\epsilon <R(A_i;q')$, it must be true that $i\leq \abs{A\backslash A_{i}}$. We now claim that $i+1\leq \abs{A\backslash A_{i+1}}$, for which it suffices to show that $A_{i+1}\subsetneq A_i$. This is true since $q'\in\mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$, and hence the set $\{ n\in A_i : q'\mid n \textrm{ and }(q',n/q')=1\}$ is not empty.
nodes.statement_short: Remove a bad prime power's elements

nodes.name: Inductive hypothesis
nodes.statement: Suppose the proposition is true for $i\geq 0$, with associated $A_i,Q_i$. We will now prove it for $i+1$.

nodes.name: All local sums large
nodes.statement: If it is true that, for all $q'\in\mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$, we have $\epsilon <R(A_i;q')$, then we let $A_{i+1}=A_i$ and $Q_{i+1}=Q_i$.

nodes.name: Remove bad q'
nodes.statement: Otherwise, let $q'\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$ be such that $R(A_i;q')\leq \epsilon$, set $A_{i+1} = A_i\backslash \{ n\in A_i : q'\mid n \textrm{ and }(q',n/q')=1\}$, and $Q_{i+1}=Q_i\cup \{q'\}$.

nodes.name: Verify
nodes.statement: It remains to verify the required properties. That $Q_{i+1}\subseteq \mathcal{Q}_A$ follows from $Q_i\subseteq \mathcal{Q}_A$ and $q'\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_i}\subseteq \mathcal{Q}_A$ (using the general fact that if $B\subseteq A$ then $\mathcal{Q}_B\subseteq \mathcal{Q}_A$).

nodes.name: Point (1)
nodes.statement: For point (1), since $A_{i+1}\subseteq A_i$, and hence $\mathcal{Q}_{A_{i+1}}\subseteq \mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$, it suffices to show that $q'\not\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_{i+1}}$. If this were not true, there would be some $n\in A_{i+1}$ such that $q'\mid n$ and $(q',n/q')=1$, contradiction to the definition of $A_{i+1}$.

nodes.name: Point (2)
nodes.statement: For point (2), we note that \[R(A_{i+1})= R(A_i)-\sum_{\substack{n\in A_i\\ q'\mid n\\ (q',n/q')=1}}\frac{1}{n} = R(A_i)-\frac{1}{q'}R(A_i;q')\geq R(A_i)-\epsilon \frac{1}{q'},\] and point (2) follows from induction and the observation that \[\frac{1}{q'}+\sum_{q\in Q_i}\frac{1}{q}=\sum_{q\in Q_{i+1}}\frac{1}{q},\] since $q'\in\mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$ and hence $q'\not\in Q_{i}$.

nodes.name: Point (3)
nodes.statement: Finally, for point (3), we note that since we assume that it is not true that for all $q'\in\mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$, we have $\epsilon <R(A_i;q')$, it must be true that $i\leq \abs{A\backslash A_{i}}$. We now claim that $i+1\leq \abs{A\backslash A_{i+1}}$, for which it suffices to show that $A_{i+1}\subsetneq A_i$. This is true since $q'\in\mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$, and hence the set $\{ n\in A_i : q'\mid n \textrm{ and }(q',n/q')=1\}$ is not empty.

nodes.name: Inductive claim
nodes.statement: We will prove the following, for all $N$ sufficiently large, real $0<M<N$, reals $\epsilon>0$ and $\alpha > 4\epsilon\log\log N$ and finite sets $A\subseteq [M,N]$ such that $R(A)\geq \alpha$ and $R(A;q)> \epsilon$ for all $q\in\mathcal{Q}_A$, by induction: for all $i\geq 0$ there exists $A_i\subseteq A$ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $R(A_i)\geq \alpha-1/M$, \item $R(A_i;q) > \epsilon$ for all $q\in\mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$, and \item either $i\leq \abs{A\backslash A_i}$ or $R(A_i)<\alpha$.

nodes.name: Deduce lemma
nodes.statement: Given this claim, we prove the lemma as follows. Let $A'\subseteq A$ be as given by Lemma~\ref{lem:pisqa}, so that the hypotheses of the inductive claim are satisfied for $A'$. We now apply the inductive claim, and choose $B=A_{\abs{A}+1}$, noting that the first alternative of point (3) cannot hold.
nodes.statement_short: Prune with Lemma pisqa, then apply the claim

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: It remains to prove the inductive claim. The base case $i=0$ is immediate by hypotheses, choosing $A_0=A$.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: We now fix some $i\geq 0$, with associated $A_i$ as above, and prove the claim for $i+1$. If $R(A_i)<\alpha$ then we set $A_{i+1}=A_i$. Otherwise, we have $R(A_i)\geq \alpha$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:pisqa} there exists $B\subset A_i$ such that \[R(B)\geq R(A_i)-4\epsilon\log\log N\geq \alpha - 4\epsilon\log\log N>0\] and $2\epsilon < R(B;q)$ for all $q\in \mathcal{Q}_B$. In particular, since $R(B)>0$, the set $B$ is not empty. Let $x\in B$ be arbitrary, and set $A_{i+1}=A_i\backslash \{x\}$. We note that since $x\in B\subseteq A$, we have $x\geq M$, and hence $R(A_{i+1})=R(A_i)-1/x\geq \alpha-1/M$, so point (1) is satisfied. Furthermore, since $R(A_i)\geq \alpha$, we have $i\leq \abs{A\backslash A_i}$, and hence $i+1 \leq \abs{A\backslash A_{i+1}}$ and point (3) is satisfied. For point (2), let $q\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_{i+1}}\subseteq \mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$. If it is not true that $q\mid x$ and $(q,x/q)=1$ then \[R(A_{i+1};q) = R(A_i; q)>\epsilon.\] Otherwise, if $q\mid x$ and $(q,x/q)=1$, then $q\in\mathcal{Q}_B$. It follows that, since $B\subseteq A_i$, we have \[R(A_{i+1};q)\geq R(B;q)-\frac{q}{x}>2\epsilon -\frac{q}{M}\geq \epsilon,\] since $q\leq \epsilon M$. The inductive claim now follows.
nodes.statement_short: Remove one element at a time

nodes.name: Already below alpha
nodes.statement: We now fix some $i\geq 0$, with associated $A_i$ as above, and prove the claim for $i+1$. If $R(A_i)<\alpha$ then we set $A_{i+1}=A_i$.

nodes.name: Remove an element
nodes.statement: Otherwise, we have $R(A_i)\geq \alpha$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:pisqa} there exists $B\subset A_i$ such that \[R(B)\geq R(A_i)-4\epsilon\log\log N\geq \alpha - 4\epsilon\log\log N>0\] and $2\epsilon < R(B;q)$ for all $q\in \mathcal{Q}_B$. In particular, since $R(B)>0$, the set $B$ is not empty. Let $x\in B$ be arbitrary, and set $A_{i+1}=A_i\backslash \{x\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Use Lemma pisqa to find $B$; remove some $x\in B$

nodes.name: Points (1) and (3)
nodes.statement: We note that since $x\in B\subseteq A$, we have $x\geq M$, and hence $R(A_{i+1})=R(A_i)-1/x\geq \alpha-1/M$, so point (1) is satisfied. Furthermore, since $R(A_i)\geq \alpha$, we have $i\leq \abs{A\backslash A_i}$, and hence $i+1 \leq \abs{A\backslash A_{i+1}}$ and point (3) is satisfied.

nodes.name: Point (2), q not dividing x
nodes.statement: For point (2), let $q\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_{i+1}}\subseteq \mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$. If it is not true that $q\mid x$ and $(q,x/q)=1$ then \[R(A_{i+1};q) = R(A_i; q)>\epsilon.\]

nodes.name: Point (2), q dividing x
nodes.statement: Otherwise, if $q\mid x$ and $(q,x/q)=1$, then $q\in\mathcal{Q}_B$. It follows that, since $B\subseteq A_i$, we have \[R(A_{i+1};q)\geq R(B;q)-\frac{q}{x}>2\epsilon -\frac{q}{M}\geq \epsilon,\] since $q\leq \epsilon M$. The inductive claim now follows.
nodes.statement_short: Local sum drops by at most $q/M\le\epsilon$

nodes.name: Apply usingq
nodes.statement: Let $I$ be any interval of length $\leq MN^{-2/(\log\log N)}$, and let $q\in\mathcal{Q}_A$ such that $R(A_I;q)> 1/2(\log N)^{1/100}$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:usingq} with $A$ replaced by $A_I$, and $k=\frac{\log\log N}{\log 2+\log\log\log N}$, so that $(\log N)^{1/k}=2\log\log N$. We choose $N$ large enough such that $k\leq c\log\log N$ (where $c$ is the constant in the statement of Lemma~\ref{lem:usingq}) and such that $\log k\geq 5000$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma usingq to $A_I$ with a specific $k$

nodes.name: Large qd_q
nodes.statement: This produces some $d_q$ such that $qd_q>\abs{I}$ and $\omega(d_q)<\tfrac{1}{1000}\log\log N$, and \[\sum_{\substack{n\in A_I\\ qd_q\mid n\\ (qd_q,n/qd_q)=1}}\frac{qd_q}{n}\gg \frac{1}{(\log N)^{1/100}(\log\log N)^2}\geq \frac{1}{(\log N)^{1/99}},\] assuming $N$ is sufficiently large.
nodes.statement_short: Get $d_q$ with $qd_q>|I|$ and large local sum

nodes.name: Define A_I^(q)
nodes.statement: Let \[A_I^{(q)}=\{ n/qd_q : n\in A_I\textrm{ with }qd_q\mid n\textrm{ and }(qd_q,n/qd_q)=1\}\] so that, the above inequality states that $R(A_I^{(q)})\geq (\log N)^{-1/99}$.

nodes.name: omega bounds
nodes.statement: We now claim that $2\log\log N\geq \omega(m) \geq \tfrac{97}{99}\log\log N$ for all $m\in A_I^{(q)}$. This follows from the trivial $\omega(mqd_q)\geq \omega(m)\geq \omega(mqd_q)-\omega(qd_q)$, and that $2\log\log N\geq \omega(mqd_q)\geq \frac{99}{100}\log\log N$ (since $mqd_q\in A$) and $\omega(qd_q)\leq 1+\omega(d_q)<\frac{1}{500}\log\log N$.

nodes.name: Apply rtop
nodes.statement: We now apply Lemma~\ref{lem:rtop} with $\epsilon=2/99$. This implies that \[\sum_{r\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_I^{(q)}}}\frac{1}{r}\geq \frac{95}{99}e^{-1}\log\log N\geq 0.35\log\log N.\]

nodes.name: x(n)
nodes.statement: By definition of $A_I$, every $n\in A_I$ with $qd_q\mid n$ must divide some $x\in I$, say $x(n)$.

nodes.name: Common multiple
nodes.statement: We claim that $x(n)=x(m)$ for all $n,m\in A_I$ with $qd_q\mid n$ and $qd_q\mid m$. Otherwise $\abs{x(q,n)-x(q,m)}$ is a non-zero multiple of $qd_q$, so $\abs{I}<qd_q\leq \abs{x(q,n)-x(q,m)}$, which is an integer in $[1,\abs{I})$, a contradiction. Let $x_q\in I$ be such that $x(q,n)=x_q$ for all $n\in A_I$ with $qd_q \mid n$.

nodes.name: Inclusion claim
nodes.statement: We claim that $\mathcal{Q}_{A_I^{(q)}}\subset \{ r\in \mathcal{Q}_A : r\mid x_q\}$, which concludes the proof using the above bound.

nodes.name: r in Q_A
nodes.statement: If $r\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_I^{(q)}}$ then there exists some $m\in A_I^{(q)}$ such that $r\mid m$ and $(r,m/r)=1$. Let $m=n/qd_q$ where $n\in A$ with $qd_q\mid n$ and $(qd_q,n/qd_q)=(qd_q,m)=1$. Certainly $r\mid n = mqd_q$, since $r\mid m$. Furthermore, $r$ is coprime to $qd_q$ since $r$ divides $m$. Therefore $(r,n/r)=(r,(m/r)qd_q)=(r,m/r)=1$, and hence $r\in \mathcal{Q}_A$.

nodes.name: r divides x_q
nodes.statement: Finally, we need to show that $r\mid x_q$. Let $m\in A_I^{(q)}$ be such that $r\mid m$. Let $n\in A_I$ be such that $qd_q\mid n$ and $m=n/qd_q$. Then $r\mid n=mqd_q$, and hence since $n\mid x_q$ we have $r\mid x_q$ as required.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Let $I$ be any interval of length $\leq MN^{-2/(\log\log N)}$, and let $A_I$ be those $n\in A$ that divide some element of $I$, and $\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{D}_I(A;M/2(\log N)^{1/100})$. We may assume that $\abs{A\backslash A_I}< M/\log N$.

nodes.name: Define E
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{E}$ be the set of those $q\in\mathcal{Q}_A$ such that $R(A_I;q)> 1/2(\log N)^{1/100}$, so that by Lemma~\ref{lem:good_d} we have $\mathcal{D}\subset \mathcal{E}$.

nodes.name: Find multiples
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:find_multiples} for each $q\in\mathcal{E}$ there exists $x_q\in I$ such that $q\mid x_q$ and \[\sum_{\substack{r\mid x_q\\ r\in \mathcal{Q}_A}}\frac{1}{r}\geq 0.35\log\log N.\]
nodes.statement_short: Each $q\in\mathcal{E}$ has a multiple $x_q\in I$ with many prime powers

nodes.name: Assume |X|>=3
nodes.statement: Let $X=\{x_q : q\in \mathcal{E}\}$. Suppose that $\abs{X}\geq 3$, and say $x,y,z\in X$ are three distinct elements. Then \[\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_A}\frac{1}{q}\geq \sum_{\substack{q\mid x\\ q\in \mathcal{Q}_A}}\frac{1}{q}+\sum_{\substack{q\mid y\\ q\in \mathcal{Q}_A}}\frac{1}{q}+\sum_{\substack{q\mid z\\ q\in \mathcal{Q}_A}}\frac{1}{q}-\sum_{q\mid (x,y)}\frac{1}{q}-\sum_{q\mid (y,z)}\frac{1}{q}-\sum_{q\mid (x,z)}\frac{1}{q},\] where the last three sums are restricted to prime powers.

nodes.name: Mertens upper bound
nodes.statement: Since $\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_A}\frac{1}{q}\leq (1+o(1))\log\log N\leq 1.01\log\log N$, say, by Lemma~\ref{lem:mertens1}, it follows that \[\sum_{q\mid (x,y)}\frac{1}{q}+\sum_{q\mid (y,z)}\frac{1}{q}+\sum_{q\mid (x,z)}\frac{1}{q}\geq 0.04\log\log N.\]
nodes.statement_short: Pairwise gcd sums must be large

nodes.name: Close integers
nodes.statement: But since $x,y\in I$ we have, by Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}, \[\sum_{q\mid (x,y)}\frac{1}{q}\ll \log\log\log N,\] and similarly for the other sums, and so the left-hand side is $O(\log\log\log N)$, which is a contradiction for large enough $N$.

nodes.name: |X|<=2
nodes.statement: Therefore $\abs{X}\leq 2$. If $\mathcal{D}$ is empty the second conclusion trivially holds, and therefore we may assume there is some $q\in \mathcal{E}$ and hence some $x_q\in X$, so $\abs{X}\geq 1$.

nodes.name: |X|=1
nodes.statement: If $\abs{X}=1$ then we are in the second conclusion, letting $x$ be the unique element of $X$, since by construction $x=x_q$ for all $q\in \mathcal{D}$, and hence in particular $q\mid x$ for all $q\in \mathcal{D}_I$ as required.

nodes.name: |X|=2
nodes.statement: Finally, we deal with the case $\abs{X}=2$. Say $X=\{w_1,w_2\}$ with $w_1\neq w_2$ (and both are elements of $I$). Let $A^{(i)}=\{n\in A: n\mid w_i\}$ and $A^{(0)}=A\backslash (A^{(1)}\cup A^{(2)})$. Without loss of generality, label the $w_i$ such that $R(A^{(1)})\geq R(A^{(2)})$.

nodes.name: Small A^(0)
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $R(A^{(0)})<R(A)/3$. In this case, since $R(A^{(0)})+R(A^{(1)})+R(A^{(2)})\geq R(A)$, we have $R(A^{(1)})\geq R(A)/3$. Furthermore, note that \[\sum_{\substack{q\mid w_1\\ q\in \mathcal{Q}_A}}\frac{1}{q}\leq \sum_{q\leq N}\frac{1}{q}-\sum_{\substack{q\mid w_2\\ q\in \mathcal{Q}_A}}\frac{1}{q}+\sum_{q\mid (w_1,w_2)}\frac{1}{q}.\] As above, by Lemma~\ref{lem:mertens1}, the assumed lower bound on the sum over $q\mid w_2$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}, for sufficiently large $N$ the right-hand side is \[\leq \brac{1.01-0.35+0.01}\log\log N\leq \tfrac{2}{3}\log\log N.\] Every $q\mid \mathcal{Q}_{A^{(1)}}$ is in $\mathcal{Q}_A$ and divides $w_1$, and hence \[\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_{A^{(1)}}}\frac{1}{q}\leq\frac{2}{3}\log\log N,\] and we are in case (1) with $B=A^{(1)}$.

nodes.name: Large A^(0)
nodes.statement: Finally, suppose that $R(A^{(0)})\geq R(A)/3$. We will derive a contradiction, assuming $N$ is large enough. Let $A'\subset A^{(0)}$ be the set of those $n\in A_I\cap A^{(0)}$ such that if $n\in A_q$ then $q\in\mathcal{E}$. By definition of $\mathcal{E}$ and Mertens' estimate \ref{lem:mertens1}, and the earlier assumption that $\abs{A\backslash A_I}<M/\log N$, \[R(A^{(0)}\backslash A')\leq \frac{\abs{A\backslash A_I}}{M}+\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_A\backslash \mathcal{E}}\frac{1}{q}R(A_I;q)\ll \frac{\log\log N}{(\log N)^{1/100}},\] and so in particular, since $R(A)\geq (\log N)^{-1/101}$, we have $R(A')\gg (\log N)^{-1/101}$.

nodes.name: Pigeonhole
nodes.statement: In particular, $\abs{A'}\gg M/(\log N)^{-1/101}$. Every $n\in A'$ divides some $x\in I$, and there are at most $MN^{-2/\log\log N}$ many $x\in I$, so by the pigeonhole principle there must exist some $x\in I$ (necessarily $x\neq w_1$ and $x\neq w_2$ since $A'\subset A^{(0)}$) such that, if $A''=\{ n\in A' : n\mid x\}$, then \[\abs{A''}\gg N^{2/\log\log N}(\log N)^{-1/101},\] and hence $\abs{A''}\geq N^{3/2\log\log N}$, say, assuming $N$ is sufficiently large.
nodes.statement_short: Many elements divide a single $x\in I$

nodes.name: Divisor bound
nodes.statement: However, if $n\in A''$ then both $n\mid x$ and $n\mid w_1w_2$ (since every $q$ with $n\in A_q$ is in $\mathcal{E}$ and so divides either $w_1$ or $w_2$), and hence $n$ divides \[(x,w_1w_2)\leq (x,w_1)(x,w_2)\leq \abs{x-w_1}\abs{x-w_2}\leq N^2.\] Therefore the size of $A''$ is at most the number of divisors of some fixed integer $m\leq N^2$, which is at most $N^{(1+o(1))2\log 2/\log\log N}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:divisor_bound}, and hence we have a contradiction for large enough $N$, since $2\log 2< 3/2$.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Let $I$ be any interval of length $\leq MN^{-2/(\log\log N)}$, and let $A_I$ be those $n\in A$ that divide some element of $I$, and $\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{D}_I(A;M/2q(\log N)^{1/00})$. We may assume that $\abs{A\backslash A_I}< M/\log N$.

nodes.name: Find multiples
nodes.statement: By Lemmas~\ref{lem:find_multiples} and \ref{lem:good_d} for each $q\in\mathcal{D}$ there exists $x_q\in I$ such that $q\mid x_q$ and \[\sum_{\substack{r\mid x_q\\ r\in \mathcal{Q}_A}}\frac{1}{r}\geq 0.35\log\log N.\]

nodes.name: Assume |X|>=2
nodes.statement: Let $X=\{x_q : q\in \mathcal{D}\}$. Suppose that $\abs{X}\geq 2$, and say $x,y\in X$ are two distinct elements. Then \[\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_A}\frac{1}{q}\geq \sum_{\substack{q\mid x\\ q\in \mathcal{Q}_A}}\frac{1}{q}+\sum_{\substack{q\mid y\\ q\in \mathcal{Q}_A}}\frac{1}{q}-\sum_{q\mid (x,y)}\frac{1}{q},\] where the third sum is restricted to prime powers.

nodes.name: gcd sum large
nodes.statement: Using our assumed bounds, this implies \[\sum_{q\mid (x,y)}\frac{1}{q}\geq \brac{0.7-\frac{2}{3}}\log\log N\geq \frac{1}{100}\log\log N,\] say.

nodes.name: Close integers
nodes.statement: But since $x,y\in I$ we have, by Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}, \[\sum_{q\mid (x,y)}\frac{1}{q}\ll \log\log\log N,\] which is a contradiction for large enough $N$.

nodes.name: |X|<=1
nodes.statement: Therefore $\abs{X}\leq 1$. If $\mathcal{D}$ is empty then the second conclusion trivially holds, for any $x\in I$.

nodes.name: Unique x
nodes.statement: Therefore there exists some $q\in \mathcal{D}$, therefore there exists some $x_q\in X$, and hence $\abs{X}=1$. Let $x\in I$ be the unique element of $X$. By construction $x=x_q$ for all $q\in \mathcal{D}$, and hence in particular $q\mid x$ for all $q\in \mathcal{D}_I$ as required.

nodes.name: Define t_i
nodes.statement: In the proof below, we write $t_i=\min(\lceil y\rceil +i, \lfloor w\rfloor)$ for all integer $i\geq 0$ for simplicity.

nodes.name: Properties of t_i
nodes.statement: It is convenient to note at the outset that $t_0=\lceil y\rceil$, $t_i\leq w$ for all $i$, for all $i\geq 0$ we have $t_{i+1}\in [t_i,t_i+1]$, and if $t_i< \lfloor w\rfloor$ then $t_{i+1}=t_i+1$. Furthermore, if $i\geq \lfloor w\rfloor -\lceil y\rceil$, then $t_i=\lfloor w\rfloor$.

nodes.name: Inductive claim
nodes.statement: We will prove by induction on $i$ that, under the same hypotheses as in the lemma, for all $0\leq i$ there exists $ A_i\subseteq A$ and integer $d_i$ with $y\leq d_i\leq t_i$ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $R(A_i) \in [2/d_i-1/M, 2/d_i)$, \item for all $q\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$ we have $R(A_i;q)> \epsilon$, \item there are no multiples of any $m\in [y,d_i)$ in $A$, and \item either there exists a multiple of $d_i$ in $A_i$, or nothing in $A_i$ is divisible by any $d\in [y,t_i]$.

nodes.name: Claim statement and point (1)
nodes.statement: We will prove by induction on $i$ that, under the same hypotheses as in the lemma, for all $0\leq i$ there exists $ A_i\subseteq A$ and integer $d_i$ with $y\leq d_i\leq t_i$ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $R(A_i) \in [2/d_i-1/M, 2/d_i)$,

nodes.name: Point (2)
nodes.statement: for all $q\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_i}$ we have $R(A_i;q)> \epsilon$,

nodes.name: Point (3)
nodes.statement: there are no multiples of any $m\in [y,d_i)$ in $A$, and

nodes.name: Point (4)
nodes.statement: either there exists a multiple of $d_i$ in $A_i$, or nothing in $A_i$ is divisible by any $d\in [y,t_i]$.
nodes.statement_short: A multiple of $d_i$ or none up to $t_i$

nodes.name: Deduce lemma
nodes.statement: Given this inductive claim, the lemma follows by letting $A' = A_{\lfloor w\rfloor -\lceil y\rceil}$ and $d=d_{\lfloor w\rfloor -\lceil y\rceil}$, so that then $t_{\lfloor w\rfloor -\lceil y\rceil}=\lfloor w\rfloor$, noting that the assumptions imply that $2/d-1/M\geq 2/w-1/M>0$ and hence $R(A')>0$ and so $A'\neq\emptyset$, and furthermore by assumption the second alternative of point (3) cannot hold. It remains to prove the inductive claim.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: For the base case $i=0$, we set $d_0=\lceil y\rceil$ and apply Lemma~\ref{lem:pisq} with $\alpha=2/d_0$ to find some $A_0\subseteq A$ such that $R(A_0)\in[2/d_0-1/M,2/d_0)$ and for all $q\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_0}$ we have $\epsilon < R(A_0;q)$. (To see that point (4) holds, note that $d_0$ is the unique integer in $[y,t_0]$.)

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: For the inductive step, suppose that $A_i,d_i$ are as given for $i\geq 0$. If there exists a multiple of $d_i$ in $A_i$, then we set $d_{i+1}=d_i$ and $A_{i+1}=A_i$. If not, then nothing in $A_i$ is divisible by any $d\in [y,t_i]$. We now set $d_{i+1}=t_{i+1}$ and apply Lemma~\ref{lem:pisq} to $A_i$ with $\alpha=2/d_{i+1}$. To be able to apply this, we need to verify that \[\alpha=2/d_{i+1}> 4\epsilon\log\log N\] and \[R(A_i)\geq \alpha+2\epsilon\log\log N= 2/d_{i+1}+2\epsilon\log\log N.\] For the first, we note that $d_{i+1}\leq w$, and hence we are done since $2/w>4/w^2\geq 6\epsilon\log\log N$. For the second, we note that by assumption, every $n\in A$ is divisible by some $d\in [y,w]$, and hence since we are assuming that nothing in $A_i$ is divisible by any $d\in [y,t_i]$, we must have $t_i<\lfloor w\rfloor$, and hence $d_{i+1}=t_{i+1}=t_i+1\geq d_i+1$. Therefore \[R(A_i)\geq \frac{2}{d_i}-\frac{1}{M}\geq \frac{2}{d_{i+1}-1}-\frac{1}{M}\geq \frac{2}{d_{i+1}-1}-\epsilon\log\log N,\] since $1/M \leq \epsilon\log\log N$, and furthermore \[\frac{2}{d_{i+1}-1}-\frac{2}{d_{i+1}}=\frac{2}{d_{i+1}(d_{i+1}-1)}\geq \frac{2}{d_{i+1}^2}\geq \frac{2}{w^2}\geq 3\epsilon\log\log N,\] and hence $R(A_i)\geq \alpha+2\epsilon\log\log N$ as required. Thus we can apply Lemma~\ref{lem:pisq}, to produce some $A_{i+1}\subseteq A_i$ such that $R(A_{i+1})\in [2/d_{i+1}-1/M,2/d_{i+1})$, such that for all $q\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_{i+1}}$ we have $R(A_{i+1};q)>\epsilon$. Furthermore, if there is something in $A_{i+1}$ divisible by some $d\in [y,t_{i+1}]$, then since $A_{i+1}\subseteq A_i$ there must be something in $A_{i+1}$ divisible by some $d\in [y,t_{i+1}]\backslash [y,t_i]$. Since $t_{i+1}\in [t_i,t_i+1]$, the only integer that could be in $[y,t_{i+1}]\backslash [y,t_i]$ is $t_{i+1}=d_{i+1}$, and the proof is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Move to $d_{i+1}=t_{i+1}$ and reapply Lemma pisq

nodes.name: Multiple present
nodes.statement: For the inductive step, suppose that $A_i,d_i$ are as given for $i\geq 0$. If there exists a multiple of $d_i$ in $A_i$, then we set $d_{i+1}=d_i$ and $A_{i+1}=A_i$.

nodes.name: No multiple
nodes.statement: If not, then nothing in $A_i$ is divisible by any $d\in [y,t_i]$. We now set $d_{i+1}=t_{i+1}$ and apply Lemma~\ref{lem:pisq} to $A_i$ with $\alpha=2/d_{i+1}$. To be able to apply this, we need to verify that \[\alpha=2/d_{i+1}> 4\epsilon\log\log N\] and \[R(A_i)\geq \alpha+2\epsilon\log\log N= 2/d_{i+1}+2\epsilon\log\log N.\]
nodes.statement_short: Set $d_{i+1}=t_{i+1}$; need hypotheses of Lemma pisq

nodes.name: First hypothesis
nodes.statement: For the first, we note that $d_{i+1}\leq w$, and hence we are done since $2/w>4/w^2\geq 6\epsilon\log\log N$.

nodes.name: Second hypothesis
nodes.statement: For the second, we note that by assumption, every $n\in A$ is divisible by some $d\in [y,w]$, and hence since we are assuming that nothing in $A_i$ is divisible by any $d\in [y,t_i]$, we must have $t_i<\lfloor w\rfloor$, and hence $d_{i+1}=t_{i+1}=t_i+1\geq d_i+1$. Therefore \[R(A_i)\geq \frac{2}{d_i}-\frac{1}{M}\geq \frac{2}{d_{i+1}-1}-\frac{1}{M}\geq \frac{2}{d_{i+1}-1}-\epsilon\log\log N,\] since $1/M \leq \epsilon\log\log N$, and furthermore \[\frac{2}{d_{i+1}-1}-\frac{2}{d_{i+1}}=\frac{2}{d_{i+1}(d_{i+1}-1)}\geq \frac{2}{d_{i+1}^2}\geq \frac{2}{w^2}\geq 3\epsilon\log\log N,\] and hence $R(A_i)\geq \alpha+2\epsilon\log\log N$ as required.

nodes.name: Apply pisq
nodes.statement: Thus we can apply Lemma~\ref{lem:pisq}, to produce some $A_{i+1}\subseteq A_i$ such that $R(A_{i+1})\in [2/d_{i+1}-1/M,2/d_{i+1})$, such that for all $q\in \mathcal{Q}_{A_{i+1}}$ we have $R(A_{i+1};q)>\epsilon$. Furthermore, if there is something in $A_{i+1}$ divisible by some $d\in [y,t_{i+1}]$, then since $A_{i+1}\subseteq A_i$ there must be something in $A_{i+1}$ divisible by some $d\in [y,t_{i+1}]\backslash [y,t_i]$. Since $t_{i+1}\in [t_i,t_i+1]$, the only integer that could be in $[y,t_{i+1}]\backslash [y,t_i]$ is $t_{i+1}=d_{i+1}$, and the proof is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma pisq and verify point (4)

nodes.name: Apply precursor
nodes.statement: Let $M=N^{1-1/\log\log N}$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:techmainprec} with $w=z/4$ and $\epsilon=N^{-5/\log\log N}$ to find some corresponding $A'$ and $d$.

nodes.name: Case (2)
nodes.statement: Suppose first that case (2) of Proposition~\ref{prop:tech_iterative} holds for $A'$. The hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{prop:fourier} are now met with $k=d$, $\eta=1/2(\log N)^{1/100}$, and $K=MN^{-2/\log \log N}$. This yields some $S\subset A'\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1/d_j$ as required.

nodes.name: Case (1)
nodes.statement: Otherwise, Proposition~\ref{prop:tech_iterative} yields some $B\subset A'$ such that \[R(B)\geq 2/3d_j-1/M\geq 1/2d_j+(\log N)^{-1/200}\] and where $\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_B}\frac{1}{q}\leq \frac{2}{3}\log\log N$.

nodes.name: Second application
nodes.statement: We apply Lemma~\ref{lem:techmainprec} again, with $y=4d$ and $w=z$, to produce some corresponding $B'\subset B$ and $d'\in [4d,z]$. Since $\sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}_{B'}}\frac{1}{q}\leq \sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_B}\frac{1}{q}\leq \frac{2}{3}\log\log N$ we can apply Proposition~\ref{prop:tech_iterative2}. The hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{prop:fourier} are now met with $k=d'$ and $\eta,K$ as above, and thus there is some $S\subset B'\subset A$ such that $R(S)=1/d'$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Reapply precursor, then iterative2 and the Fourier proposition
